slides.heading: The nervous system
slides.body_md: Part 1: the cells, the divisions, the brain and the spinal cord.

visual.alt: Pathway from stimulus to receptor, central nervous system and effector

slides.narration: Every response of the body, from a blink to solving a problem, begins with a stimulus that a receptor detects. The message travels along nerves to the central nervous system, which decides and sends orders to muscles and glands.

slides.heading: Structure of a neuron
slides.body_md: A **neuron** has a **cell body (cyton)** with a nucleus and **Nissl granules**, branched **dendrites** that receive impulses, and one **axon** that carries impulses away. The axon is wrapped by **myelin** (from Schwann cells) with gaps called **nodes of Ranvier**, and ends in **axon terminals**.

slides.narration: Dendrites bring impulses toward the cell body, and the axon carries them away. The fatty myelin sheath insulates the axon, and the gaps between its segments are the nodes of Ranvier. The tip of each branch of the axon ends in a small swelling that meets the next cell.

slides.heading: Neurons and nerves
slides.body_md: A **nerve** is a bundle of axons wrapped in connective tissue. Nerves can be sensory, motor or mixed.

rows: From receptors to the central nervous system
From the central nervous system to muscles and glands

visual.alt: Table of sensory, motor and mixed nerves

slides.narration: Sensory nerves carry information in, motor nerves carry commands out, and mixed nerves contain both kinds of fibre. All the spinal nerves are mixed.

slides.heading: Types of neurons
slides.body_md: Neurons are classified by the number of processes that leave the cell body.

slides.heading: Divisions of the nervous system
slides.body_md: The **central nervous system (CNS)** is the brain and spinal cord. The **peripheral nervous system (PNS)** is all the nerves outside, divided into **somatic** (to skeletal muscles) and **visceral or autonomic** (to internal organs).

visual.alt: Tree of the divisions of the human nervous system

slides.narration: The brain and spinal cord form the central system. All nerves outside it are the peripheral system. Its somatic part controls voluntary muscles, and its autonomic part controls the heart, glands and smooth muscles without our will.

slides.heading: The autonomic nervous system
slides.body_md: The visceral nervous system has two parts that act in opposite ways on most organs.

visual.alt: Table comparing sympathetic and parasympathetic effects

slides.narration: The sympathetic part prepares the body for fight or flight, so the pupils widen and the heart races. The parasympathetic part restores calm, slows the heart and promotes digestion.

slides.heading: Parts of the brain and their functions
slides.body_md: Each part has its own job, but they work together.

rows: Thinking, memory, voluntary movement, speech, sensation, vision, hearing
Relay station for sensory and motor signals
Body temperature, hunger, thirst, emotions; controls the pituitary
Reflexes of sight and hearing (corpora quadrigemina)
Balance, posture and smooth, coordinated movement
Links parts of the brain; helps control breathing
Centres for heartbeat, breathing and blood pressure; swallowing, coughing, vomiting

visual.alt: Table of brain parts and functions

slides.narration: The cerebrum is the seat of intelligence and voluntary action. The cerebellum keeps balance. The medulla controls the vital automatic functions of heartbeat and breathing, so damage to it is very serious.

slides.heading: T.S. of the spinal cord
slides.body_md: In T.S. the **grey matter** (cell bodies) is butterfly-shaped with **dorsal and ventral horns** around the **central canal**, and the **white matter** (myelinated fibres) lies outside. The **dorsal root** (sensory, with a **ganglion**) and the **ventral root** (motor) join to form a **spinal nerve**.

slides.heading: The reflex arc
slides.body_md: A **reflex** is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus, controlled by the spinal cord without waiting for the brain.

visual.alt: Reflex arc from receptor to sensory neuron, relay neuron, motor neuron and effector

slides.narration: In a withdrawal reflex, a sensory neuron carries the message to the spinal cord, a relay neuron passes it on, and a motor neuron makes the muscle contract. The brain is told afterwards.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: time taken by a reflex
slides.body_md: A person steps on a thorn. The sensory and motor fibres are each 0.9 m long and conduct at 60 m per second; there are 2 synapses, each causing a delay of 0.5 ms. Find the time for the reflex arc.
bullets: Each fibre: $\dfrac{0.9}{60} = 0.015$ s $= 15$ ms.
Synaptic delays $= 2 \times 0.5 = 1$ ms.

visual.alt: Worked table: 31 milliseconds

slides.narration: Divide the length of each fibre by its speed, double it for the sensory and motor sides, and add the small delay at each synapse. The whole reflex takes only about three hundredths of a second.

slides.body_md: Work out the conduction time in one fibre of the arc.
slides.narration: Quick check. Divide distance by speed.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Neuron: dendrites, cell body with nucleus and Nissl granules, axon with myelin and nodes of Ranvier, axon terminals.
Types: unipolar, bipolar, pseudounipolar, multipolar.
Nervous system: CNS (brain, spinal cord); PNS (12 cranial, 31 spinal pairs); somatic and autonomic (sympathetic, parasympathetic).
Brain: cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus; midbrain; pons, cerebellum, medulla oblongata.
Spinal cord: grey and white matter, dorsal and ventral roots; reflex arc.

visual.alt: Summary table of brain and cord functions

slides.narration: To recap: neurons receive and send impulses, the central system integrates them, and the peripheral system carries them. Each part of the brain has a special role, and the spinal cord handles reflexes quickly without help from the brain.

bullets: Label a neuron: **dendrite, cell body, nucleus, axon, myelin sheath, node of Ranvier, axon terminal**.

slides.heading: The nerve impulse
slides.body_md: Part 2: how a neuron fires and how it passes the message on.

visual.alt: Resting potential, depolarisation, repolarisation and synapse

slides.narration: A nerve impulse is a wave of electrical change along the membrane of a neuron. It depends on the movement of sodium and potassium ions across the membrane.

slides.heading: Resting potential
slides.body_md: A resting axon is **polarised**: the inside is negative and the outside positive, about **-70 mV**. Potassium ions leak out more easily than sodium ions leak in, and the **sodium-potassium pump** moves **3 sodium ions out for every 2 potassium ions in**.

visual.alt: Table of ion distribution across the resting membrane

slides.narration: At rest, sodium is mostly outside and potassium inside. Potassium leaks out more freely than sodium leaks in, and the pump moves three sodium ions out for every two potassium ions in. So the inside becomes negative.

slides.heading: The action potential
slides.body_md: A stimulus that brings the membrane to the **threshold (-55 mV)** opens **sodium channels**: sodium floods in and the potential rises to about **+30 mV** (**depolarisation**). Then potassium channels open and potassium leaves, so the potential falls back (**repolarisation**).

slides.narration: The curve shows the electrical event at one point on the axon. The membrane rises very quickly when sodium enters, then falls as potassium leaves, dips slightly below the resting level and returns to rest as the pump restores the ions.

slides.heading: Ion movements in each phase
slides.body_md: The action potential is **all or none**: once threshold is reached, it has the same size every time.

rows: Sodium channels open; sodium rushes in
Sodium channels close; potassium channels open; potassium leaves
Pump restores sodium outside and potassium inside

visual.alt: Table of ion movements in each phase of the action potential

slides.narration: Sodium entry causes the rise, and potassium exit causes the fall. Afterwards the pump puts the ions back. Once the membrane has fired, it cannot fire again for a very short time, called the refractory period.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: potentials and the pump
slides.body_md: The resting potential is -70 mV, the threshold is -55 mV and the peak is +30 mV. Find (i) the amplitude of the action potential, (ii) the depolarisation needed to reach threshold, and (iii) the ions moved by the pump in 500 cycles.
bullets: Amplitude $= 30 - (-70) = 100$ mV.
To threshold: $-55 - (-70) = 15$ mV.
In 500 cycles: sodium out $= 3 \times 500 = 1500$; potassium in $= 2 \times 500 = 1000$; net positive charge out $= 500$.

visual.alt: Worked table: amplitude 100 millivolts

slides.narration: Subtract the resting value from the peak to get the full height of the impulse. The pump removes more positive charge than it brings in, which helps keep the inside of the cell negative.

slides.heading: Myelinated and non-myelinated fibres
slides.body_md: Myelination speeds up conduction and also saves energy.

rows: Spinal and cranial nerves, white matter

visual.alt: Table comparing myelinated and non-myelinated fibres

slides.narration: Because ions cross only at the nodes, a myelinated fibre needs far less pumping to restore the balance after each impulse. Thick myelinated fibres carry fast messages such as those to skeletal muscles.

Non-myelinated: $\dfrac{0.6}{1} = 0.6$ s $= 600$ ms; ratio $= 100$.

slides.narration: Divide the length by the speed for each fibre. In this model the myelinated fibre is one hundred times faster. Real speeds vary with fibre thickness, but myelinated fibres are always much faster.

slides.body_md: Transmission at a chemical synapse takes place in one direction only.

slides.narration: The impulse triggers calcium entry, which releases the transmitter. The transmitter crosses the gap, opens channels in the next cell and starts a new potential. It is then broken down, for example by an enzyme, so the signal ends.

bullets: Resting potential about -70 mV: potassium leak and the sodium-potassium pump (3 sodium out, 2 potassium in).
Action potential: threshold -55 mV, sodium in (depolarisation to +30 mV), potassium out (repolarisation); all or none.
Myelinated fibres: saltatory conduction at nodes of Ranvier; faster and cheaper.
Chemical synapse: calcium, vesicles, transmitter, cleft, receptors; one-way.

sections.heading: 1. Neurons and nerves
sections.body_md:
The **neuron** is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system.
- **Cell body (cyton or soma):** contains the **nucleus** and **Nissl granules** (rough endoplasmic reticulum with ribosomes, concerned with protein synthesis).
- **Dendrites:** short, branched processes that **receive** impulses and carry them **towards** the cell body.
- **Axon:** a long process that carries impulses **away** from the cell body. It begins at the **axon hillock**; its membrane is the axolemma and its cytoplasm the axoplasm. In a **myelinated fibre** the axon is wrapped in a **myelin sheath** (formed by **Schwann cells** in the peripheral nervous system), with gaps called **nodes of Ranvier**. The axon ends in branches that carry **axon terminals (synaptic knobs)** with synaptic vesicles.

**Types of neuron (by number of processes)**
| Type | Processes | Where found |
|---|---|---|
| Unipolar | One process from the cell body | Embryonic stage; some invertebrates |
| Bipolar | One axon and one dendrite, at opposite ends | Retina of the eye, lining of the nose, inner ear |
| Pseudounipolar | A single process that divides into two branches near the cell body | Dorsal root ganglia (sensory neurons) |
| Multipolar | One axon and several dendrites | Cerebral cortex, motor neurons of the spinal cord |

*Note on books:* some books group the pseudounipolar neuron with the unipolar type and then list unipolar neurons in the dorsal root ganglia; this chapter follows the four-type scheme of the syllabus.

**Nerves:** a **nerve** is a bundle of axons held together by connective tissue. **Sensory (afferent)** nerves carry impulses from receptors to the central nervous system, **motor (efferent)** nerves carry impulses from it to muscles and glands, and **mixed** nerves contain both.

sections.heading: 2. Divisions of the human nervous system
sections.body_md:
- **Central nervous system (CNS):** the **brain** (in the cranial cavity) and the **spinal cord** (in the vertebral canal).
- **Peripheral nervous system (PNS):** all the **nerves** outside the CNS: **12 pairs of cranial nerves** from the brain and **31 pairs of spinal nerves** from the cord (8 + 12 + 5 + 5 + 1: cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, coccygeal), 43 pairs in all.
  - Functionally the PNS has an **afferent (sensory)** and an **efferent (motor)** division.
  - The efferent division is the **somatic nervous system** (to **skeletal muscles**, voluntary) and the **visceral or autonomic nervous system** (to **smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands**, involuntary).
- **Autonomic nervous system:** **sympathetic** (prepares the body for emergencies: increases heart rate, dilates pupils, widens air passages, slows digestion) and **parasympathetic** (restores and conserves: slows the heart, constricts pupils, stimulates digestion). Most organs receive both, and the two have opposite effects.

key_terms.definition_md: Brain and spinal cord.
Cranial and spinal nerves outside the CNS.
Involuntary control of internal organs; sympathetic and parasympathetic parts.

sections.heading: 3a. The human brain
sections.body_md:
The brain is protected by the **skull** and by three membranes, the **meninges**: the outer **dura mater**, the middle **arachnoid** and the inner **pia mater**, which is in contact with the brain. **Cerebrospinal fluid** lies in the space below the arachnoid and in the brain's ventricles.

**Forebrain**
- **Cerebrum:** the largest part, in two **hemispheres** joined by the **corpus callosum**. The outer **cortex** is **grey matter** (cell bodies) with the **frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes**: thinking, memory, voluntary movement and speech (frontal), general sensation (parietal), hearing and memory (temporal), vision (occipital). The inner part is white matter.
- **Thalamus:** relay station for sensory and motor signals to and from the cortex.
- **Hypothalamus:** controls **body temperature, hunger, thirst**, emotions and the **pituitary** gland; it has neurosecretory cells. (The limbic system, with the amygdala and hippocampus, is concerned with emotion and memory.)

**Midbrain:** the **corpora quadrigemina** (four swellings) control reflex movements of the eyes and head in response to sight and sound.

**Hindbrain**
- **Cerebellum:** **balance, posture and coordination** of voluntary movement.
- **Pons:** fibre tracts linking parts of the brain; helps to regulate breathing.
- **Medulla oblongata:** centres for **heartbeat, breathing and blood pressure** and for reflexes such as swallowing, coughing, sneezing and vomiting; it continues as the spinal cord.

The midbrain, pons and medulla form the **brain stem**.

Controls temperature, hunger, thirst and the pituitary.
Balance, posture and coordination.

sections.heading: 3b. The spinal cord and the reflex arc
sections.body_md:
The **spinal cord** lies in the vertebral canal and is protected by the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid. In **T.S.** the **grey matter**, rich in cell bodies, is **butterfly-shaped** with **dorsal (posterior) horns** and **ventral (anterior) horns** around the **central canal**; the **white matter** around it is made of **myelinated fibres** in tracts. The **dorsal root** carries **sensory** fibres into the cord and bears a **dorsal root ganglion** (cell bodies of the sensory neurons); the **ventral root** carries **motor** fibres out. The two roots join to form a mixed **spinal nerve**.

**Functions:** (i) the centre of **reflex actions**; (ii) **conduction** of impulses between the body and the brain.

**Reflex action:** a quick, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus, carried out by the **reflex arc**: **receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron (in the grey matter) → motor neuron → effector**. In a withdrawal reflex the brain is told only afterwards. For example, with fibres 0.9 m long at 60 m per s and two synapses of 0.5 ms each, the arc takes 31 ms in the model used in this chapter.

Carries motor fibres out of the spinal cord.

sections.heading: 4. Generation and conduction of the nerve impulse; the synapse
sections.body_md:
**Resting potential:** a neuron at rest is **polarised**: the **inside is negative** (about -70 mV) and the outside positive. The membrane is much more permeable to **potassium** than to **sodium**, so potassium leaks out; negatively charged proteins stay inside; and the **sodium-potassium pump** uses ATP to move **3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in** in each cycle.

**Action potential:** a stimulus that reaches the **threshold** (about -55 mV) opens **voltage-gated sodium channels**. Sodium rushes in and the membrane **depolarises** to about **+30 mV** (the inside becomes positive). Sodium channels then close and **potassium channels open**, so potassium leaves and the membrane **repolarises**, often undershooting slightly (about -76 mV, hyperpolarisation) before the pump restores the resting state. The action potential is **all or none**, and for a short time (the **refractory period**) the membrane cannot respond to a new stimulus; a refractory period of 2 ms limits the rate to 500 impulses per second.

**Conduction:** the depolarised region sets up **local currents** that depolarise the next region.
- **Non-myelinated fibre:** the impulse passes **continuously**, point by point: **slow**.
- **Myelinated fibre:** the myelin **insulates** the axon, so ions can cross only at the **nodes of Ranvier**; the impulse **jumps from node to node** (**saltatory conduction**), which is **much faster** (in this chapter, 100 m per s against 1 m per s) and uses less energy.

**Synaptic transmission:** the junction between two neurons is a **synapse**. In an **electrical synapse** the membranes are very close and current flows directly through gap junctions (very fast, either way, rare in humans). In a **chemical synapse** the **pre-synaptic** terminal, with **synaptic vesicles**, is separated from the **post-synaptic** membrane by the **synaptic cleft**. An impulse opens calcium channels; calcium entry makes the vesicles **fuse with the membrane and release the neurotransmitter** (for example **acetylcholine**); it diffuses across the cleft and binds **receptors**, opening ion channels and generating a **post-synaptic potential** (excitatory or inhibitory). The transmitter is then **broken down** (acetylcholine by acetylcholinesterase) or taken back. Transmission is **one-way**.

*Note on books:* the resting potential is quoted as −60 to −90 mV and conduction speeds vary widely; -70 mV, +30 mV, 100 and 1 m per s are the round values used for calculation in this chapter.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying dendrites carry impulses away from the cell body (they carry them towards it).
- Placing the pseudounipolar neuron in the brain (it is in the dorsal root ganglion).
- Swapping the roots: the **dorsal** root is **sensory** with the ganglion; the **ventral** root is **motor**.
- Saying the impulse is conducted faster in myelinated fibres "because myelin is a good conductor" (it is an insulator; the impulse jumps between nodes).
- Reversing the ions: depolarisation is **sodium in**; repolarisation is **potassium out**.
- Saying the sodium-potassium pump moves 2 sodium out and 3 potassium in (it is 3 out, 2 in).
- Writing that the transmitter crosses the cleft in both directions (one way only).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a part of the neuron or brain, a type of neuron with location, the ion that moves, a give-a-reason.
- 2–3-mark questions: types of neurons; sympathetic and parasympathetic; functions of brain parts; resting and action potentials; saltatory conduction; synaptic transmission.
- 5-mark questions in parts: neuron with a labelled diagram; brain; T.S. of spinal cord with reflex arc; nerve impulse and synapse.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a bipolar neuron from a multipolar neuron by their processes, and give one place where each is found.

answer.model_answer_md: A **bipolar** neuron has **one axon and one dendrite**, at opposite ends of the cell body; it is found in the **retina** or the lining of the nose. A **multipolar** neuron has **one axon and several dendrites**; it is found in the **cerebral cortex** and as the motor neurons of the spinal cord.

questions.solution_md: Processes; locations.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish sensory, motor and mixed nerves by the direction in which they carry impulses, and give an example of a mixed nerve.

answer.model_answer_md: **Sensory (afferent)** nerves carry impulses **from receptors to the central nervous system**. **Motor (efferent)** nerves carry impulses **from the central nervous system to muscles or glands**. **Mixed** nerves contain **both sensory and motor fibres** and carry impulses in both directions; the **spinal nerves** are mixed nerves.

questions.solution_md: Three kinds; example.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a myelinated multipolar neuron. [2]
(b) State the function of the dendrites, the axon and the myelin sheath. [2]
(c) Name the type of neuron in which several dendrites arise from the cell body, and give one place where it is found. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** a cell body with a **nucleus** and **Nissl granules**, branched **dendrites**, an **axon** with the **axon hillock**, **myelin sheath** segments separated by **nodes of Ranvier**, and **axon terminals**.

(b) **Dendrites** receive impulses and carry them to the cell body; the **axon** carries impulses **away** from it; the **myelin sheath** **insulates** the axon and makes conduction faster.

(c) A **multipolar** neuron, for example in the **cerebral cortex**.

questions.solution_md: Labelled neuron; functions; multipolar.

questions.stem_md: Watching a thrilling film, a student notices that her pupils widen, her heart beats faster and her mouth goes dry, without any decision on her part. These changes are produced mainly by the

options.text_md: sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system
parasympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system

questions.solution_md: Emergency responses are produced by the sympathetic division — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which of these actions is controlled by the somatic neural system?

options.text_md: Raising a hand to answer a question
Narrowing of the pupil in bright light
Movement of food along the intestine
Slowing of the heart during sleep

questions.solution_md: The somatic system supplies skeletal muscles under voluntary control — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Nerves that emerge directly from the brain, 12 pairs in a human, are called
questions.solution_md: 12 pairs of cranial nerves arise from the brain — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A man dozes off after a heavy lunch. Which change is brought about mainly by the parasympathetic division?

options.text_md: Increased movement and secretion in the digestive tract

questions.solution_md: The parasympathetic division promotes digestion; the other changes are sympathetic — option (b).

questions.stem_md: How many pairs of spinal nerves arise from the cervical, thoracic and lumbar regions of the cord together?
How many individual nerves, counting those on both sides of the body, leave the brain and spinal cord of a human?
questions.solution_md: Pairs $= 12 + 31 = 43$; nerves $= 2 \times 43 = 86$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Stimulation of the parasympathetic nerves to the heart slows the heartbeat.

**Reason (R):** The parasympathetic division prepares the body for fight or flight.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: it is the sympathetic division that prepares the body for fight or flight; the parasympathetic division restores calm — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Name the two divisions of the efferent peripheral nervous system and state which organs each supplies.

answer.model_answer_md: The **somatic nervous system** carries impulses to the **skeletal muscles**, which are under voluntary control. The **visceral (autonomic) nervous system** carries impulses to the **smooth muscles, cardiac muscle and glands** of the internal organs, which work involuntarily.

questions.solution_md: Somatic and visceral with targets.

questions.stem_md: Compare the effects of the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions on the pupil, the heart and the digestive tract.

answer.model_answer_md: The **sympathetic** division **dilates the pupil**, **raises the heart rate** and **slows digestion**, preparing the body for emergencies. The **parasympathetic** division **constricts the pupil**, **slows the heart** and **stimulates digestion**, restoring and conserving energy. The two usually have **opposite effects** on the same organ.

questions.solution_md: Three organs, two divisions.

questions.solution_md: Breathing, heartbeat and blood pressure are controlled from the medulla — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which part of the brain links the nervous system with the endocrine system by controlling the pituitary gland?
questions.solution_md: The hypothalamus controls the pituitary — option (b).

questions.solution_md: The midbrain’s corpora quadrigemina control reflexes to sight and sound — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which meninx is thin, rich in blood vessels and in direct contact with the surface of the brain?

questions.stem_md: A girl touches a cactus spine and her hand jerks away. Which sequence correctly shows the pathway?

options.text_md: Skin receptor → motor neuron → relay neuron → sensory neuron → muscle
Muscle → sensory neuron → cerebrum → motor neuron → skin
Skin receptor → cerebrum → relay neuron → muscle only
Skin receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron in the spinal cord → motor neuron → muscle

questions.solution_md: A reflex arc runs from receptor through sensory, relay and motor neurons to the effector — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a road accident, only the dorsal roots of the nerves of one leg are cut. The patient will

options.text_md: feel the leg normally but be unable to move it
lose all sensation in the leg but still be able to move it voluntarily
lose both sensation and movement in the leg

questions.solution_md: Dorsal roots carry sensory fibres into the cord; motor fibres in the ventral roots are intact — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The sensory fibre of a reflex arc is 0.9 m long and conducts impulses at 60 m per second. How long does an impulse take to travel along it, in milliseconds?

In a withdrawal reflex, a sensory fibre and a motor fibre, each 0.9 m long, conduct at 60 m per second. The impulse crosses 2 synapses, and each adds 0.5 ms. How long does the whole reflex arc take, in milliseconds?

**Assertion (A):** In a transverse section of the spinal cord, the grey matter lies inside the white matter.

**Reason (R):** Grey matter is made mainly of nerve cell bodies, whereas white matter is made mainly of myelinated nerve fibres.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; the arrangement follows from the composition: cell bodies are inside and fibre tracts outside — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The narrow channel in the centre of the spinal cord that contains cerebrospinal fluid is the ______ canal.
questions.solution_md: Central canal.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The thalamus is a part of the hindbrain.
questions.solution_md: False. The thalamus is part of the forebrain.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: The cerebral cortex looks grey, but the outer part of the spinal cord looks white.

answer.model_answer_md: The cortex is rich in **nerve cell bodies**, whereas the outer spinal cord is made of **myelinated nerve fibres**, and myelin is white.

questions.solution_md: Cell bodies vs myelinated fibres.

marking_scheme.step: Cell bodies grey; myelinated fibres white

questions.stem_md: Complete the analogy: Thalamus : relay station for sensory signals :: hypothalamus : ______.

answer.model_answer_md: **Control of body temperature, hunger and thirst (and of the pituitary gland).**

questions.solution_md: Temperature, hunger, thirst.

questions.stem_md: Name the three parts of the hindbrain, and state the function of the cerebellum and of the medulla oblongata.

answer.model_answer_md: The hindbrain consists of the **cerebellum**, the **pons** and the **medulla oblongata**. The **cerebellum** controls **balance, posture and coordination of movement**; the **medulla oblongata** contains centres controlling the **heartbeat, breathing and blood pressure**.

questions.solution_md: Parts and two functions.

questions.stem_md: State two functions of the hypothalamus, and explain how it influences the pituitary gland.

answer.model_answer_md: The **hypothalamus** regulates **body temperature** and the urges for **hunger and thirst**. It has **neurosecretory cells** that make hormones; these **control the secretion of the pituitary gland**, linking the nervous and endocrine systems.

questions.solution_md: Two functions; control of pituitary.

questions.stem_md: Name the three meninges that protect the brain, in order from outside to inside, and state one function of the cerebrospinal fluid.

answer.model_answer_md: The meninges are the **dura mater** (outer, tough), the **arachnoid** (middle, web-like) and the **pia mater** (inner, thin and in contact with the brain, rich in blood vessels). The **cerebrospinal fluid** lies below the arachnoid and in the cavities of the brain; it **cushions the brain** against shocks and helps to supply it with nutrients.

questions.solution_md: Meninges in order; CSF.

questions.stem_md: Name the four lobes of the cerebral cortex and state one function of each.

answer.model_answer_md: The cerebral cortex is divided into four lobes. The **frontal lobe** controls **voluntary movement, speech and thinking**. The **parietal lobe** receives **general sensations** such as touch, pain and temperature from the body. The **temporal lobe** is concerned with **hearing and memory**. The **occipital lobe**, at the back, is the centre of **vision**.

questions.solution_md: Four lobes with functions.

questions.stem_md: Describe the arrangement of grey and white matter in a transverse section of the spinal cord, and name the two roots of a spinal nerve.

answer.model_answer_md: The **grey matter** is inside, **butterfly-shaped**, with **dorsal and ventral horns** around the **central canal**; it consists mainly of **cell bodies**. The **white matter** lies outside it and consists of **myelinated fibres**. A spinal nerve forms from a **dorsal root** (sensory, with a ganglion) and a **ventral root** (motor).

questions.solution_md: Grey inside; white outside; two roots.

questions.stem_md: A boy steps on a thorn and lifts his foot before he feels pain. Trace the path of the impulse and explain why the response is so quick.

answer.model_answer_md: Receptors in the skin send an impulse along a **sensory neuron** to the cord through the **dorsal root**; a **relay neuron in the grey matter** passes it to a **motor neuron**, which leaves through the **ventral root** and makes the leg muscle contract. The path is short and **does not wait for the brain**, so the response is **involuntary and quick**; the brain is informed afterwards.

questions.solution_md: Reflex arc and reason.

marking_scheme.step: Relay and motor neuron via ventral root
Spinal cord not brain, so quick

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a vertical section of the human brain showing the cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain, pons, cerebellum and medulla oblongata. [2]
(b) State the function of the cerebellum and of the thalamus. [2]
(c) Name the structure that joins the two cerebral hemispheres. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** the **cerebrum** with the **corpus callosum**; below it the **thalamus** and **hypothalamus** with the pituitary; the **midbrain**, **pons** and **medulla oblongata** forming the brain stem; the **cerebellum** behind the pons.

(b) The **cerebellum** controls **balance, posture and coordination** of movement; the **thalamus** is the **relay station** for sensory and motor signals going to and from the cerebrum.

(c) The **corpus callosum**.

questions.solution_md: Labelled brain; functions; corpus callosum.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a transverse section of the spinal cord showing the dorsal and ventral roots. [2]
(b) Explain, with the path of the impulse, how a reflex action such as blinking or withdrawing the hand takes place through the spinal cord. [2]
(c) State two functions of the spinal cord. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** **white matter** outside; butterfly-shaped **grey matter** with **dorsal and ventral horns** and a **central canal**; the **dorsal root** with its **ganglion**, the **ventral root**, and the **spinal nerve**.

(b) The **receptor** sends an impulse along a **sensory neuron** (dorsal root) to a **relay neuron** in the grey matter, then to a **motor neuron** (ventral root) and the **effector muscle**, which contracts without waiting for the brain.

(c) The cord is the **centre of reflexes** and **conducts impulses** between the body and the brain.

questions.solution_md: T.S. diagram; reflex arc; functions.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Receptor to sensory neuron to relay

questions.passage_md: Two patients, P and Q, each have an injury to the nerve roots of the left leg in the lower back. Both are normal on the right side. When the sole of the left foot is pricked with a pin, patient P says that she feels the pin but cannot move her foot, and patient Q moves nothing and says that he feels nothing, although he can move the foot when asked to do so.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) The ventral (motor) roots

**(b)** The **dorsal root ganglion**.

**(c)** (i) The reflex needs an impulse to reach the cord through the **sensory neurons of the dorsal root**; these are damaged, so no impulse reaches the **relay neuron** and **motor neuron**, although the motor neurons are intact and the foot can be moved **voluntarily** by the brain’s commands.

**OR** (ii) The sensory neurons carry the impulse to the cord, but the **motor neurons of the ventral root are cut**, so the impulse cannot reach the **muscle** and the **effector** does not respond; she feels the pin because the message also goes up to the **brain**.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** P feels the pin, so sensory fibres work; she cannot move, so motor fibres are cut — option (b).

**(b)** Dorsal root ganglion.

**(c)** (i) Sensory path broken.

(ii) Motor arm cut.

children.solution_md: P feels the pin, so sensory fibres work; she cannot move, so motor fibres are cut — option (b).

answer.model_answer_md: The **dorsal root ganglion**.

questions.stem_md: A student places one microelectrode inside a resting axon and another in the fluid outside it. What does the meter show?

options.text_md: The inside is about 70 mV negative to the outside
The inside is about 70 mV positive to the outside
The inside is about +30 mV to the outside

questions.solution_md: A resting axon is polarised, negative inside, about -70 mV — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Ouabain blocks the sodium-potassium pump. If a neuron is soaked in it for a long time, its resting potential will

options.text_md: gradually become less negative as the ion gradients run down

questions.solution_md: Without the pump the Na⁺ and K⁺ gradients dissipate, so the resting potential falls towards zero — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A nerve fibre is placed in a bath with a very high concentration of K⁺ outside. Its resting potential will

options.text_md: become more negative, because more K⁺ leaves the cell
become less negative, because less K⁺ leaves the cell
be unchanged, because only Na⁺ matters

questions.solution_md: The resting potential depends largely on K⁺ leaving; with K⁺ high outside, less leaves — option (b).

questions.stem_md: During the rising phase of an action potential, the membrane potential changes from the resting level to a positive value. This is mainly due to

options.text_md: entry of Na⁺ ions through voltage-gated channels
exit of K⁺ ions through leak channels

questions.solution_md: Depolarisation is caused by Na⁺ entry — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A single neuron is stimulated first at twice its threshold strength and then at ten times its threshold strength. The action potentials produced will

options.text_md: be five times larger at the stronger stimulus
be smaller at the stronger stimulus
be of the same size, but may occur more often at the stronger stimulus
not be produced at the weaker stimulus

questions.solution_md: An action potential follows the all-or-none rule; strength is coded by frequency — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In multiple sclerosis the myelin of nerve fibres in the brain and spinal cord is destroyed, and impulses become slow or fail. The best explanation is that

options.text_md: sodium ions can no longer enter the axon at all
the insulation is lost, so the impulse can no longer jump from node to node
the nodes of Ranvier become thicker
the neurotransmitter is released too quickly

questions.solution_md: Loss of myelin destroys saltatory conduction — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a myelinated nerve fibre, exchange of ions across the axon membrane takes place only at the
questions.solution_md: Myelin blocks ion exchange; it happens at the nodes — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Botulinum toxin stops the release of acetylcholine from the endings of motor neurons. The expected effect on the muscles it supplies is

options.text_md: continuous contraction, because the cleft widens
no change, because the impulse crosses the cleft directly
paralysis, because no transmitter crosses the cleft to stimulate the muscle

questions.solution_md: Without transmitter release the post-synaptic membrane is not excited — option (d).

questions.stem_md: An insecticide inhibits acetylcholinesterase. At a synapse of an insect treated with it, acetylcholine will

options.text_md: remain in the cleft and keep stimulating the post-synaptic membrane
be taken back by the post-synaptic neuron at once

questions.solution_md: The enzyme normally breaks down acetylcholine; blocking it prolongs the stimulation — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Impulses cross a chemical synapse from the pre-synaptic to the post-synaptic neuron only, and never backwards, because

options.text_md: transmitter is released only by the pre-synaptic terminal and receptors lie only on the post-synaptic membrane
the cleft is too wide for the transmitter to cross backwards
the post-synaptic neuron has no membrane
both membranes release transmitter at once

questions.solution_md: Vesicles are on one side and receptors on the other — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which ion entering the axon terminal triggers the fusion of synaptic vesicles with the membrane?
questions.solution_md: Calcium entry triggers release of the transmitter — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a short interval the sodium-potassium pumps of a small stretch of membrane move 2100 sodium ions out of the cell. How many potassium ions do they bring in?
questions.solution_md: 3 Na⁺ out for 2 K⁺ in: $\dfrac{2100}{3} \times 2 = 1400$.

questions.stem_md: An action potential starts when the membrane reaches -55 mV and rises to +30 mV. By how many millivolts does the potential rise after threshold has been reached?
After firing, a neuron cannot fire again for 4 ms (the absolute refractory period). What is the greatest number of impulses it can carry in one second?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1000}{4} = 250$ per second.

questions.stem_md: A myelinated axon 0.45 m long has a node of Ranvier every 1.5 mm. How many nodes does it have, approximately?
A touch impulse travels 1.5 m along a myelinated fibre at 100 m per second. How long does it take, in milliseconds?

**Assertion (A):** Chemical synapses allow impulses to pass in one direction only.

**Reason (R):** Acetylcholine is a neurotransmitter.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the existence of acetylcholine does not explain the one-way passage; that is due to release on one side and receptors on the other — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The inside of a resting axon is positive with respect to the outside.

**Reason (R):** The resting membrane is far more permeable to sodium ions than to potassium ions.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are false: the inside is negative, and the resting membrane is more permeable to potassium than to sodium — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft is ______.
questions.solution_md: Acetylcholinesterase.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A neurotransmitter always excites the post-synaptic neuron.
questions.solution_md: False. Some transmitters or receptors inhibit the post-synaptic neuron.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: A myelinated fibre uses less energy than a non-myelinated fibre of the same length to carry the same impulses.

answer.model_answer_md: Ions cross the membrane **only at the nodes of Ranvier**, so the **sodium-potassium pump** has far fewer ions to restore after each impulse.

questions.solution_md: Ion exchange only at nodes.

marking_scheme.step: Ions cross only at nodes, so less pumping

questions.stem_md: Explain why the inside of a resting neuron is negative compared with the outside.

answer.model_answer_md: **Potassium ions leak out** through the membrane much more easily than sodium leaks in, while **large negatively charged molecules stay inside**. The **sodium-potassium pump** also moves **three sodium ions out for two potassium ions in**, so more positive charge is removed than returned, leaving the inside **negative**.

questions.solution_md: Leak, trapped anions, pump.

marking_scheme.step: Pump moves 3 Na out and 2 K in

questions.stem_md: State which ion moves, and in which direction, during depolarisation and during repolarisation of an axon.

answer.model_answer_md: During **depolarisation**, voltage-gated **sodium channels open** and **sodium ions enter** the axon, making the inside positive. During **repolarisation**, the sodium channels close, **potassium channels open** and **potassium ions leave**, so the inside becomes negative again.

questions.solution_md: Sodium in; potassium out.

questions.stem_md: Explain why a nerve impulse travels much faster along a myelinated fibre than along a non-myelinated fibre of the same thickness.

answer.model_answer_md: The **myelin sheath insulates** the axon, so ions can cross the membrane only at the **nodes of Ranvier**. The **local current** flows through the axon from one node to the next and the impulse **jumps from node to node** (**saltatory conduction**). In a non-myelinated fibre the impulse must excite **every point** of the membrane in turn, which is **much slower**.

questions.solution_md: Insulation, nodes, saltatory vs continuous.

marking_scheme.step: Myelin insulates; ions cross at nodes

questions.stem_md: Describe how an impulse is transmitted across a chemical synapse.

answer.model_answer_md: The impulse reaches the **axon terminal**; **calcium ions** enter and make **synaptic vesicles** fuse with the membrane, releasing **neurotransmitter** into the **synaptic cleft**. It diffuses across and binds **receptors on the post-synaptic membrane**, opening ion channels and generating a new **post-synaptic potential**. The transmitter is then **broken down or taken back**.

questions.solution_md: Calcium, release, binding, removal.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between electrical and chemical synapses on three points.

answer.model_answer_md: In an **electrical synapse** the membranes are very close and **ions pass directly** through gap junctions, so transmission is **very fast** and can go **either way**; such synapses are **rare in humans**. In a **chemical synapse** there is a **synaptic cleft** and a **neurotransmitter** carries the message, so there is a **slight delay** and transmission is **one-way**; most human synapses are of this kind.

questions.solution_md: Gap, speed, direction, occurrence.

questions.stem_md: A squid axon is moved from sea water to a bath containing only one third of the normal sodium concentration. Predict the effect on its resting potential and on its action potential, and give the reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: The **resting potential changes very little**, because at rest the membrane is mainly **permeable to potassium**, not sodium. The **action potential becomes smaller**, because **less sodium** is available to **enter** the axon, so the **peak is lower** and the rise is slower; sodium entry is what causes depolarisation.

questions.solution_md: Rest unchanged; action potential smaller.

marking_scheme.step: Resting potential almost unchanged, with reason

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain how the resting potential of a neuron is maintained. [2]
(b) Describe the changes in ion movement and membrane potential when the neuron is stimulated beyond threshold. [2]
(c) What is the refractory period? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The membrane is more permeable to **potassium** than to sodium, so potassium **leaks out**; negatively charged molecules stay inside, and the **sodium-potassium pump** moves **3 sodium out and 2 potassium in** each cycle, keeping the inside about **-70 mV**.

(b) At **threshold** (-55 mV) sodium channels open and **sodium enters**, so the membrane **depolarises** to about **+30 mV**; then sodium channels close, **potassium channels open** and **potassium leaves**, so it **repolarises**, and the pump restores the resting state.

(c) The short time after firing when the membrane **cannot respond to a new stimulus**.

questions.solution_md: Resting potential; action potential; refractory period.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain saltatory conduction of a nerve impulse. [2]
(b) Compare a myelinated and a non-myelinated nerve fibre in a table of three points. [2]
(c) State one effect on conduction of the loss of myelin. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The **myelin sheath insulates** the axon, so ions cross only at the **nodes of Ranvier**; the **local current** flows from node to node and the impulse **jumps** from one node to the next.

(b) **Myelinated:** has myelin from Schwann cells; ions cross only at nodes; **fast, saltatory** conduction. **Non-myelinated:** no myelin; ions cross at every point; **slow, continuous** conduction. The myelinated fibre also **uses less energy**.

(c) Conduction becomes **slow or fails**.

questions.solution_md: Saltatory; comparison; demyelination.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Insulation and ion exchange at nodes

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a chemical synapse. [2]
(b) Describe the steps of synaptic transmission. [2]
(c) State what happens to the neurotransmitter afterwards. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** a **pre-synaptic axon terminal** with **mitochondria** and **synaptic vesicles**, the **synaptic cleft**, and the **post-synaptic membrane** with **receptors**.

(b) The impulse opens **calcium channels**; calcium makes vesicles release **neurotransmitter** into the cleft; it **diffuses across** and binds **receptors**, opening ion channels and causing a new **potential** in the post-synaptic neuron.

(c) It is **broken down** (acetylcholine by acetylcholinesterase) or **taken back** into the terminal.

questions.solution_md: Labelled synapse; steps; removal.

questions.passage_md:
A student stimulated three single fibres, X, Y and Z, of an isolated nerve and recorded how long an impulse took to cross a 0.12 m length of each.

| Fibre | Distance (m) | Time (ms) |
|---|---|---|
| X | 0.12 | 1.2 |
| Y | 0.12 | 60 |
| Z | 0.12 | 6 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 20 m per second

**(b)** (a) Fibre X, the fastest

**(c)** (i) Fibre Y is probably **thin and non-myelinated**, so the impulse must **excite every point** of the membrane in turn instead of **jumping between nodes of Ranvier**; this **continuous conduction** is slow.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** $\dfrac{0.12}{0.006} = 20$ m per second.

**(b)** X conducts at 100 m per second, the fastest, which is typical of a myelinated fibre — option (a).

**(c)** (i) Non-myelinated.

(ii) Time increases.

Which fibre is most likely thick and myelinated?

options.text_md: Fibre Z, because it is faster than Y
None, because all three are of the same length

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Suggest why fibre Y conducts so slowly.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Predict what would happen to the time recorded for fibre X if its myelin were stripped off, and explain.
